label: explain2-track-1
one_line: We test whether changing one small piece of DNA slides the point where a gene switch flips, without changing how sharply it flips.
what: Engineers build tiny switches out of genes inside bacteria. Bacteria are single living cells, like the common lab germ E. coli. A switch works like a dimmer. When the incoming signal goes up, the output goes down. Each switch has two numbers. The first is the signal level where the output is halfway down. The second is how sharply it drops, like a gentle slope versus a cliff. Engineers can edit one short piece of DNA, called the dial. Its full name is the ribosome binding site. Think of it as a landing strip. The cell's protein-making machinery lands on it and starts reading the gene. A better landing strip means the cell makes more of a protein called a repressor. A repressor is a protein that turns another gene down. Our bet is simple. Editing the dial moves the halfway point left or right. It does not change the sharpness. Picture a curve on a graph. Sliding means the same S-shaped curve moves sideways. Changing shape means the S gets steeper or flatter. We bet on sliding. We use only public tables of switches that other people already measured. We do no new lab work. Before we test on fresh data, we write down what would count as failure.
why: Suppose the bet holds. Then a designer can tune a switch with one simple edit. The designer can trust that the rest of the curve stays put. That saves a lot of trial and error. It also gives our project a clear rule to add to its law library. The law library is our list of rules that a computer has checked. It has no rule on this today. Suppose the bet fails. Then designers learn the edit has side effects. Either answer is useful. We do not claim the bet is true. The data so far say it is roughly true, but not exactly.

steps.text: Pick the switches. We use public tables of measured gene switches. They come from a free design tool called Cello. Cello is software that helps people design gene circuits. Each table lists many switches and their measured numbers.
steps.picture: Like starting from a printed catalogue of light dimmers with their test results.

steps.text: Find pairs of switches that differ only in the dial. In one table there are 10 such pairs.
steps.picture: Like finding two dimmers that are the same model except for the size of the knob.

steps.text: For each pair, compare how sharply the two drop. The biggest gap in the main table is about 16 percent. That is roughly one part in six.
steps.picture: Like checking whether two door hinges swing with the same snap. One is at most a sixth snappier.

steps.text: Compare where each one reaches halfway. These points differ by up to 7.7 times. So the dial really does something.
steps.picture: Like one dimmer needing a knob turn almost eight times bigger than the other.

steps.text: Prove the sliding idea with pure maths. A computer program that checks proofs line by line has confirmed it. The proof says this. If an edit only rescales the signal, the curve slides sideways and keeps its shape.
steps.picture: Like proving that a ruler slid along a table keeps the same gaps between its marks.

steps.text: Check the idea on a second, unrelated data set. It covers a different, well-studied bacterial protein. We redo the curve fitting for it.
steps.picture: Like asking a second shop whether their dimmers behave the same way.

steps.text: Work out the sharpness again ourselves. We start from the raw cell measurements. In those, a machine measures the glow of thousands of single cells, one by one. Our numbers agree closely with the published ones.
steps.picture: Like re-weighing a parcel on your own scale.

steps.text: Write down the pass and fail lines before opening any fresh data. The proposed lines are not yet frozen. That means they could still change.
steps.picture: Like calling your shot before you throw the dart.

steps.text: Test on the kept-back table. Report every miss, even if it hurts the idea.
steps.picture: Like showing the exam marks whether or not they are good.

wrong_if: Here is the bet. We wrote it before looking at fresh data. Take pairs that differ only in the dial. Their sharpness should differ by no more than about 25 percent. That is one part in four. The halfway point should also move a lot in at least one pair. It should shift by about 6 times or more. For example, one switch might need a signal of 1 and its partner a signal of 6. If sharpness changes by more than 25 percent, we are wrong. If the halfway point hardly moves, we are wrong too. These lines are proposals and may still change. A pass line that is too loose is a problem. In our checks, pairs with nothing in common would also pass about half the time. So the lines must be tight.
could_go_wrong: The kept-back table is mostly the same switches measured again. So it is not a truly independent test.
We read the headers and part lists of the kept-back table. So we cannot promise it is untouched.
The edit does more than slide the curve. The flat top and flat bottom of the curve also move. For one gate, the top level was 3.9, 4.1 or 6.8, depending on the dial.
Sharpness depends on how the curve is fitted. The same data give different answers under different fitting methods.
Some of our planned pass lines are so loose that unrelated pairs would pass about half the time.
Yeast is a single-cell fungus, the kind used in bread and beer. Only one yeast pair qualifies. It differs in a second part as well. So yeast tells us nothing about the idea.
A rival explanation says proteins that tie each other up could change sharpness when the protein amount changes.
The second data set uses a different kind of signal. So it supports the idea but does not confirm it.

questions.q: What exactly is the dial, and how does it set the protein amount?
questions.a: The dial is a short stretch of DNA called the ribosome binding site. It sits just before the gene. The cell's protein-making machinery latches onto it before reading the gene. A stronger landing strip means the machinery starts more often. That gives more protein. A weaker one gives less.

We do not yet know. We re-ran the sums on public files and the numbers match. In the main table the sharpness gap is at most about 16 percent. That describes past data. It is not a proof for new switches.

We have not run the Cello fitting code. We have not run the full reshuffling test, which shows how much a number could wobble. We did not test whether predicted protein amounts match the halfway shifts. We have not read most of the original papers beyond their short summaries. We have not done any new lab work.

questions.q: Why does a dimmer picture fit?
questions.a: A gene switch turns its output down smoothly as the input rises. A dimmer does the same with light. The picture shows the two numbers that matter, the halfway point and the sharpness. The picture is a help, not a proof.

questions.q: Does the maths prove the idea?
questions.a: No. The proof says one thing. If the edit only rescales the input, the curve slides and keeps its sharpness. It says nothing about whether real DNA edits do only that.

questions.q: Why is the kept-back table a problem?
questions.a: About 15 of its 18 gate names also appear in the main table. About 13 of those have identical parts. So it is partly the same switches measured again. That is like grading a student on the same questions they practised.

questions.q: Did the earlier plan have errors?
questions.a: Two. It counted 9 matching pairs where there are 10. It also said two yeast switches differed in only one part. They also differ in the part that switches on their output.

questions.q: Is there another data set that agrees?
questions.a: Yes, partly. It covers a well-studied bacterial protein called the lac repressor. A lab chemical called IPTG acts as its signal. In two cases the halfway point moved 4.9 times and 17.5 times. The sharpness changed by at most 15 percent. A third case was too flat to judge.

Yes. One theory is about proteins that tie each other up and hold each other out of action. It says sharpness can depend on protein amount. We cannot say it is the strongest rival. That ranking would be our own judgement.
It means the signal needed for the halfway drop gets about 6 times bigger or smaller. Say one switch flips halfway at a signal of 10. Its partner would then flip at about 60, or at about 1.7.

glossary.plain: A stretch of DNA that holds the recipe for one protein.
A small set of genes that turns an output up or down when a signal changes.
The long molecule in cells that stores the instructions for making proteins.
A tiny working part of a cell that does a job, such as switching a gene off.
A protein that turns another gene down.
Single-cell living things with no nucleus, such as the gut microbe E. coli.
A common lab bacterium that people use to build gene circuits.
A single-cell fungus, the kind used to make bread and beer.
The smallest living unit of an organism.
A short piece of DNA before a gene. The cell's protein-making machinery lands on it to start reading. A stronger one means more protein.
The signal level at which the output has dropped to the middle between its high and low levels.
How sharply the output changes as the signal rises. A cliff is steep. A gentle ramp is not.
The number that measures steepness of a switch curve. A bigger number means a sharper drop. In this text we just say sharpness.
A line on a graph that shows output against input.
How many times bigger or smaller a number gets. A 6-times shift means 10 becomes 60, or 10 becomes about 1.7.
Free software, plus its public tables, for designing gene circuits.
One gene switch that turns an input signal into an output signal.
Two gates that match in every part but one.
A public table that lists many gates and their measured values.
Data used to set up and tune our test before the real check.
Data that we keep unseen until the final test, so the test is fair.
To work out the curve numbers again from the raw measurements.
A way to measure the glow of thousands of single cells, one by one.
Reshuffling the data many times to see how much a number could wobble.
The DNA part that decides how strongly a gate's output gene is switched on.
A piece of DNA that tells the cell to stop reading a gene.
The flat top or flat bottom part of a curve.
A well-studied bacterial protein. A lab chemical called IPTG turns it off.
A lab chemical that acts as the signal for the lac repressor.
When one protein ties up another and holds it out of action.
A computer program that checks maths proofs line by line.
The project's list of rules that a computer has checked.
Parts in each hundred. 25 percent is one part in four.
A number we set in advance that the result must beat to count as a success.
The file format of the Cello tables. It is a plain data file.
A long code made from a file's bytes. If the file changes at all, the code changes. It lets you check you have the same file.
A kind of gut bacterium. One table covers it, but we did not open that table.

check_yourself.what: Open the main Cello table and compare its size and hash (its fingerprint code) with ours.
check_yourself.expect: Size 4834067 bytes. Hash c702d6b9b11bcd3c4fb9f7a77d24af1b549cecf3e7184b3a36692873735cd6f0. The file may change later.

check_yourself.what: Recompute the pair table for the main Cello table.
check_yourself.expect: 20 gates and 10 pair lines. The biggest sharpness gap is 0.1587, which is about 16 percent.

check_yourself.what: Check the sliding algebra and the spread in top level.
check_yourself.expect: A gap of about 1e-15, which is zero for practical purposes (a decimal point followed by 14 zeros and a 1). Also top levels of 3.9, 4.1 and 6.8 for one gate.

check_yourself.what: Check the Lean proof of the sliding rule.
check_yourself.expect: No errors, and the line reading ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx.

check_yourself.what: Check that the main paper is real.
check_yourself.expect: The title Genetic circuit design automation, in Science, 2016.

check_yourself.what: Redo the lac refit (takes about 2 to 3 minutes).
check_yourself.expect: 18 rows. Then the summary script shows a 4.94-fold shift and a sharpness gap of at most 0.116 in one case.

left_out: Claim that yeast output level (ymin) shifts up to 5.5 times in RBS-only pairs: partly verified only, the yeast figure was not checked.
Claim that 0 of 10 refit pairs have a significant sharpness difference (z above 2): not re-run by the verifier, so left out as a fact.
Claim that the sharpness test on the kept-back table is the only real test and others are redundant: the verifier called it judgement, so it is not stated as fact.
Claim that the kept-back library is still unopened: could not be checked, and the critic's own report says its headers and part lists were read.
Claim that molecular titration is the strongest rival to the idea: only partly supported, so we say only that it is a rival.
Claim that the refit of one kept-back table reaches a sharpness gap of 0.4254: only read from stored output, not re-run, so not used as a fact.
Claim that the cytometry refit is r of 0.972 against shipped values was verified, but the mismatch of scales between fit and shipped values is unexplained and is left out.
Law-set count claims (59 laws, 14 without a theorem name) were supported but are not needed here, so omitted.
One law whose title names a taxon under the holdout rule: excluded by the holdout rule.
The words orthogonal and allosteric appear only in source titles; we do not use them in the text.
changes: Defined the dial once, early in 'what': it is the ribosome binding site, a landing strip for the protein-making machinery, and more landing means more repressor (definition from the agents' reports).

Added a plain explanation of sliding versus changing shape in 'what' (same S-curve moves sideways versus S gets steeper or flatter), as the reader asked for a sliding-versus-shape picture; no graph can be drawn in this text field.
Added a new Q&A answering 'what exactly is the dial and how does it set protein amount', the question the reader could not answer.
Rewrote 'The halfway point should move by at least about 6 times' into plain words with a worked example (signal 1 versus 6), and added a Q&A and glossary entry for 'times'.
Rewrote the 'loose rule can pass for unrelated pairs' sentence into two simple sentences with the about-half figure.
Rewrote 'the edit does not only slide the curve' caveat: said what top and bottom levels are and gave the 3.9, 4.1, 6.8 figures.
Rewrote the law library sentence: it now says what the library is (rules a computer has checked) in the same place it first appears.
Rewrote the yeast caveat: says what yeast is and that the one pair also differs in a second part.
Explained 1e-15 in the check list as practically zero and tied 0.1587 to about 16 percent; explained the 3.9/4.1/6.8 values.
Explained Cello at first use as free design software with public tables; moved reading weight off the Cello name.
Replaced 'Hill number' in the main text with 'sharpness'; kept it only in the glossary, defined.
Explained flow cytometry, Lean, bootstrap (as the reshuffling test), IPTG, lac repressor, sequestration (as proteins tying each other up), repressor and yeast where they first appear.

Removed the bare terms output promoter, terminator, plateau, ymin, z above 2 from the reading path (output promoter became 'the part that switches on their output'; plateau became 'flat top and bottom'). Glossary still defines them; ymin and z are in left_out only.
Added glossary entries for UCF, hash, and fold shift, and widened the 'steepness' and 'dial' entries; noted that orthogonal and allosteric appear only in source titles.
Added a concrete comparison to each number: 16 percent is about one part in six, 25 percent is one part in four, 7.7 times is almost eight times the knob turn.
Split long sentences across 'what', 'why', 'wrong_if' and the steps into short ones; spelled out abbreviations (RBS, DNA role, E. coli) on first use.
Explained 'not yet frozen' in the pass-and-fail step as 'could still change'.
Simplified the kept-back table Q&A comparison and the 'what have you not checked' answer (no bare 'bootstrap' or 'Cello fitting' jargon without explanation).
Merged the caveats about proteins that tie up each other and the second data set into plainer sentences; kept all eight caveats.
